content: The philtrum, derived from the Greek word philtron meaning to love or to kiss, is the vertical groove located in the upper lip. It is formed during embryonic development at the junction where the nasomedial and maxillary processes meet. This anatomical feature allows humans to exhibit a broader range of lip movements, which significantly enhances both vocal and non-verbal communication. When these embryonic processes fail to fuse completely, it can result in a cleft lip, a condition sometimes referred to as a hare lip. Additionally, a flattened or smooth philtrum is a recognized clinical sign of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome, a condition caused by prenatal alcohol exposure. The ancient Greeks believed the philtrum to be one of the most erogenous zones on the human body, which is reflected in its etymology. In Jewish folklore, as described in the Talmud (Niddah 30b), it is said that God sends an angel to each unborn child to teach it all the wisdom of the world. Just before birth, the angel touches the baby between the upper lip and the nose, causing it to forget all the knowledge it has learned. This story is further elaborated in the book What the Angel Taught You by Rabbi Noah Weinberg and Yaakov Salomon. Other cultural traditions also reference the philtrum. In some sayings, it is believed that an angel shushes the baby in the womb to prevent it from speaking about heaven or to make it forget divine secrets. In other interpretations, the philtrum is thought to be an indentation left by the finger of God or the spot where an angel placed its finger to silence the child after revealing a secret. This concept was notably referenced in the film The Prophecy by the character of the archangel Gabriel, played by Christopher Walken.
